'''Mary A. Clem''' (née '''Mary A. McLaughlin'''; 1905{{Spaced en dash}}1979)<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|date=2014|title=Mary Clem in the U.S., Social Security Death Index, 1935-2014|url=https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/3693/|url-access=subscription|website=Ancestry.com|publisher=[[Social Security Death Index]], Master File. [[Social Security Administration]]|quote=Birth Date: 19 Oct 1905, Death Date: Jan 1979, Last Residence: 50010, Ames, Story, Iowa, USA}}</ref> was an American [[mathematician]], and a [[Computer (job description)|human computer]]. She was a staff member at [[Iowa State University]], and was recognized for inventing the “zero check” technique for detecting errors.

== Biography ==
Clem was born on October 19, 1905<ref name=":2" /> in the small town of [[Nevada, Iowa|Nevada]], in [[Story County, Iowa|Story County]], central [[Iowa]]. She completed her high school degree and found employment for several years with the [[Iowa Department of Transportation|Iowa State Highway Commission]] and [[Iowa State University|Iowa State College]] as a computing clerk, auditing clerk, and bookkeeper.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Mary A. Clem|url=https://plaza.las.iastate.edu/directory/mary-a-clem/|access-date=2020-09-21|website=Plaza of Heroines|publisher=Iowa State University (ISU)|language=en-US}}</ref>

In 1931, she joined the Mathematics Statistical Service of the Mathematics Department of Iowa State College to work as a human computer under the supervision of [[George W. Snedecor|George Snedecor]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Grier|first=David Alan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YTcDAQAAQBAJ|title=When Computers Were Human|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2007|isbn=978-0-691-13382-9|location=Princeton, NJ|pages=159–174}}</ref> Although she complained that mathematics was her poorest subject in high school, she was fascinated with figures and data. Most of her work was done via [[Punched card|punch cards]], both creating formulas and cards, and running accuracy checks on them. She invented the “zero check” while working in Snedecor’s lab. The “zero check” is a sum that should equal zero if all other numbers had been correctly calculated.<ref name=":1" /> These sums helped check for errors in computing algorithms.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Lamb|first=Gregory M.|date=2005-07-05|title=Before computers, there were these humans...|work=Christian Science Monitor|url=https://www.csmonitor.com/2005/0705/p15s01-bogn.html|access-date=2020-11-05|issn=0882-7729}}</ref> Clem expressed that her lack of training as a mathematician is what made her notice these sums, as they had often been overlooked by others.<ref name=":1" /> In 1940, Clem was advanced to be technician and chief statistical clerk in charge of the Computing Service of the Statistical Laboratory.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news|date=1957-03-10|title=Mechanical brain goes to college|pages=23|work=The Gazette|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/62603877/mechanical-brain-goes-to-college/|access-date=2020-11-05}}</ref> In 1962, she transferred to the new Computation Center at Iowa State University.<ref name=":0" />

Clem went on the 2nd Allied Mission to Greece in 1946 as a junior statistician, and there she observed the elections.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news|date=1946-11-04|title=Iowa-born sampling world-famous|pages=8|work=The Des Moines Register|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/62604542/iowa-born-sampling-world-famous/|access-date=2020-11-05}}</ref> In 1952, she was a statistical consultant to the [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission]] in [[Hiroshima]], Japan.<ref name=":0" />
